Hi Rafael,

Thanks again for the call this morning. As part of our internal compliance review ahead of procurement sign-off, we need a compact evidence package showing that a Dedicated deployment can be pinned to physical host boundaries and that tenant data can be proven erased on demand. Could you provide the following by Oct 7?

1) A diagram or short PDF that maps tenant binding to physical hosts (or host pools) and explains network/storage isolation at a high level.
2) The retention policy and snapshot lifecycle for a pinned Dedicated tenant (how long snapshots persist, where they are stored).
3) The wipe/runbook we would expect your ops team to run for an erasure request, plus average timelines observed (RTO/RPO-ish).
4) A small metrics export (CSV) with snapshot timestamps, creation/expiration, and any IOPS/throughput counters you can share for the past 90 days.
5) Any attestation language you can provide (draft is fine) we can include in our security questionnaire.

If anything above is sensitive, tell us what you can safely share and what requires an NDAs or an on-site/controlled review.

Appreciate it — this will help unblock procurement.

Best,
Elena Morales
Head of Security Programs
FinWell

Subject: Boundary diagram + quick runbook (draft)

Hi Elena / Rafael,

Attached: boundary_diagram_v2.pdf (diagram) and runbook_excerpt.txt (inline excerpt below).

Summary (high-level):
- Dedicated tenants are scheduled to specific host pools; host pools are groups of bare-metal or isolated GPU nodes logically bound at provisioning time. We do not place third-party tenant data on the same physical host where a pinned tenant is running.
- Snapshots are stored on a region-local object store with tenant-scoped prefixes. Replication is region-only for Dedicated by default; cross-region replication only happens if the customer explicitly enables multi-region DR.
- Retention: automatic incremental snapshots are retained for 30 days by default; customers can request longer retention up to 365 days for an additional fee. Snapshots are garbage-collected after expiry; metadata entries are removed and underlying blocks are queued for secure deletion.

Wipe/runbook excerpt:
1) Validate tenant identifier and scope of erasure (compute cache vs. persistent snapshot).
2) Quiesce tenant and freeze writes.
3) Trigger snapshot deletion job for tenant-scoped prefixes (record snapshot IDs).
4) Zero-out metadata pointers and issue block-level secure-delete on storage backends (internal async job).
5) Verify deletion in snapshot_log and generate erasure report with timestamps.
6) Provide signed attestation if required by customer.

Estimated times: snapshot deletion job completes within 5–15 min for metadata removal; secure-delete background block purge is dependent on storage subsystem, typical completion seen in 2–24 hours for small tenants, and up to 72 hours for very large datasets (we document results in the erasure report).

If you need a formal runbook doc (ops-playbook) we can produce that as a redacted PDF for vendor review.

Laura Bennett
Principal Infrastructure Engineer, Redwood Inference

(Attachments: boundary_diagram_v2.pdf)

Elena — thanks for the questions. Quick answers and next steps: 

1) Snapshot scope: logs we shared cover persistent snapshot objects and tenant-scoped object-store prefixes. Ephemeral caches (in-memory and transient compute caches) are not captured in snapshot logs; those are cleared as part of the quiesce + wipe sequence. Laura: we will add an explicit note in the runbook excerpt about cache flush and process for confirming cache eviction.

2) Attestation: Kimberly — can Legal/Contracts draft a short signed attestation PDF (template already lives in shared drive) confirming wipe guarantees and typical timelines? If legal needs redlines, Rafael will coordinate — FinWell requested the attestation by Oct 7; we can aim to deliver a signed PDF by Oct 6 if legal approves the template.
